title: What the Mass Remembers
author: Lantern Original
summaryTr: Bir yerleşimden kurtarılan insanların ve o yerleşimin son arşivinin bulunduğu yük gemisi, güvenli bir buluşma için yeterince yavaşlayamaz. Seyrüsefer uzmanı Eda, yolcuların yaşamını korurken geçmişten neyin kurtarılacağına kimin karar vereceğiyle yüzleşir.
paragraphs: The first thing Eda Sorel noticed was the absence of vibration. For eleven days the salvage vessel Parallax had shuddered around her like an elderly animal enduring a difficult journey. Now the deck beneath her boots was unnaturally still. In the navigation display, their projected rendezvous with the relief carrier became a close approach, then a miss. The computer did not use the word disaster. It preferred insufficient braking reserve, a description whose restraint Eda found personally offensive.

Captain Irin called from propulsion before the alarm sounded. A fragment shed by the outer shielding had punctured the reserve tank. Its contents were streaming behind them in a pale fan that looked, through the inspection camera, almost ornamental. The isolation valve had closed. It had also isolated most of the propellant they needed, on the wrong side of the rupture. They were carrying forty-seven people, one sleeping dog and the municipal archive of Vesper Station. None of those things would survive another circuit through the debris belt ahead.

The relief carrier could receive them if they matched its velocity at the rendezvous plane. It could not come farther in. Its great habitat drums had neither the acceleration nor the shielding for the belt, and the smaller rescue boats were already committed to other vessels. The carrier's commander stated these limitations without apology. Eda preferred that to sympathy. She asked for their final permissible arrival corridor and laid it across her display: a narrow volume of space, six hours away, that seemed an absurdly small place to put a future.

Irin came onto the bridge carrying a pressure gauge she had removed from its socket. She set it beside Eda, an obsolete gesture of verification. 'Tell me the options before you tell me the recommendation.' Eda ran the model again. They could burn what remained and arrive too fast. They could coast and miss the carrier entirely. Or they could feed nine tonnes of material through the conversion drive, whose chamber reduced suitable matter to a controllable reaction stream. The only compatible material aboard was the archive.

Vesper had stored its records in laminated ceramic plates. The medium was durable, compact and resistant to the intermittent power failures that had finally made the station uninhabitable. Its other useful property was unfortunate: once stripped of their protective frames, the plates were excellent conversion feedstock. Bas Neri, the archivist, had calculated the mass himself when they loaded the ship. Eda remembered his pleasure at finding an unexpected margin in the cargo allowance. He had brought an additional cabinet of oral histories because there had been room.

The archive weighed twelve tonnes. Nine would have to disappear into the drive. The figure already accounted for the ship becoming lighter as it consumed the plates; it was not a rough estimate that could be improved by remembering a clever principle. Eda checked the model against the manual tables. Irin checked it independently. Then they sat without speaking while the cooling pumps resumed their ordinary hum. Somewhere below them, a child was practising a tune on a plastic recorder, getting the same three notes wrong with unwavering confidence.

Bas arrived with a data slate tucked beneath his arm. He was sixty-eight and dressed as though a committee might unexpectedly inspect his cuffs. Eda explained the failure. He listened to the whole account, including the requirement for nine tonnes, then asked whether the cargo restraints counted. They did not. Their alloy would foul the conversion chamber. Neither would the ship's hull, the water supply or the furniture serve as usable feedstock. The emergency drive had been built for a particular class of industrial cargo. Their luck consisted of having that cargo and their misfortune of needing it.

'There are death certificates in those cabinets,' Bas said. 'And ownership records. And the testimony from the ventilation inquiry.' Eda knew. Her mother's final statement was in the inquiry collection, describing the maintenance contractor's decision to disable alarm thresholds. The company had dismissed that testimony as uncorroborated. Three weeks later, Vesper's central habitat had become impossible to ventilate. The evacuation had cost lives before the wider station failure began. Eda had taken this navigation contract partly to ensure that the records reached a place where somebody would have to read them.

Bas asked about copying the archive. The answer was less straightforward. The plates stored data as patterns through their depth. Reading them required a calibrated phase oscillator, and the archive's normal reader had been destroyed during loading. Parallax had one compatible oscillator in its guidance unit. They could disconnect it and improvise a reader at the feed throat. The computer could then decode each plate immediately before the drive destroyed it. But the guidance unit would lose the component it needed to coordinate the braking pulses precisely.

Their portable storage had ample capacity. Capacity was not the bottleneck. Nor was transmission: once decoded, files could be sent to the carrier through the directional link. The bottleneck was the single oscillator and the cooling capacity around it. Switching it repeatedly between reading and guidance would require recalibration, taking longer than their remaining flight. They had to decide which task it would perform during the burn. Eda explained this twice, because every person aboard would naturally think of copying, and nobody should be asked to accept a sacrifice concealed behind jargon.

Irin authorised a trial. While Eda computed a burn sequence that could be controlled manually, Bas and the propulsion engineer, Fen, carried a plate to the workshop. It contained drainage inspections from a district that no longer existed. Bas handled it with the same care he gave the oral histories. Fen removed a strip from its edge and ran it through the test reader. A three-dimensional map appeared on her slate, followed by a complaint about a leaking ceiling. They had recovered the contents. The physical strip crumbled when she touched it.

The result established possibility, not adequacy. At that rate they could read less than half the mass they needed to consume before reaching the rendezvous plane. Feeding the plates faster would destroy patterns before the oscillator resolved them. Feeding them slowly enough to preserve everything would leave them travelling too fast to dock. Eda asked Fen to test overlapping passes. The next strip produced a file with every fourth segment missing. Its reconstruction software invented a drainage pipe through a bedroom. Bas turned off automatic repair. 'A plausible record is not a surviving record,' he said.

They could save three tonnes intact and decode another portion during the burn. The rest would be lost. The amount recovered would depend on how many unread plates they interleaved with the slower scanning passes to maintain thrust. Eda built a schedule around the drive's minimum stable flow. If anything went wrong, the scanner would have to be bypassed immediately. Irin insisted on a physical lever that could do this without software permission. Bas watched Fen install it. He did not object, but his hands remained folded tightly enough to whiten the knuckles.

Manual guidance was the other uncertainty. Parallax's old optical sight had survived because nobody had considered it worth removing. Eda could use the carrier's beacon as a reference and adjust the pulses from calculated tables. Her instructors had taught the method as a historical exercise. The examination had allowed three attempts and a quiet room in which to review mistakes afterwards. She had practised it; she had never used it with people depending on the outcome. The distinction occupied her thoughts more than she wanted to admit.

They ran a simulation with the archive reader drawing its predicted power. For the first forty seconds Eda held the ship inside the corridor. Then a delay in the actuator response made her overcorrect. The simulated vessel crossed the carrier's plane beyond the receiving envelope. A red annotation appeared on the display. Fen, watching from the workshop, said they should use automatic guidance and accept the loss. She was not being unimaginative. She had seen the actual heat damage in the actuators, which the software model represented with a tidy probability distribution.

Eda asked for one more trial, this time with Irin calling the table entries and Fen reporting actuator lag in real time. They did not improve because Eda became more gifted. They improved because the task stopped being hers alone. Irin anticipated the next correction; Fen identified a sticking valve before Eda compensated in the wrong direction. They reached the receiving envelope with a small margin. On a third trial, using the least favourable measured lag, they did so again. Irin authorised the conversion. The authority did not make her look relieved.

They had four hours left. Bas wanted to begin selecting plates immediately, but Irin called a meeting in the passenger compartment. The forty-four evacuees who were not crew had a right to know what would happen to the cargo they had helped carry aboard. There would be no vote on whether to sacrifice passengers for documents. Irin made that boundary explicit. There would be a decision about how the recoverable portion was chosen, and about whether anyone with a personal stake should control that choice. Eda found herself looking at her own hands.

The compartment smelled of warm fabric, disinfectant and the orange sweets somebody had distributed to the children. Bas explained the archive's structure. Its public catalogue survived on his slate, so they knew what each cabinet contained. Some plates held thousands of short records; others held a few hours of dense testimony. Files were grouped into context bundles, preserving the links between a claim, its source and its subsequent corrections. Saving isolated fragments might produce more readable words while making those words less trustworthy. The archive was not a heap of interchangeable memories.

A former station manager proposed preserving the legal records first. A nurse asked whether patient histories counted as legal records. A young woman who had lost her father asked why maintenance reports should outrank the last recording of a person's voice. A man near the door wanted everything concerning the ventilation contractor saved, because otherwise the deaths would become nobody's fault. His argument was Eda's own. Hearing it spoken in that room, beside people with different losses, made it less self-evidently universal than it had sounded in her head.

Bas had prepared a priority list. It favoured official proceedings, engineering plans and records likely to establish rights after relocation. The list was defensible. It also reproduced the station's old hierarchy with unnerving fidelity: the people who had generated the most paperwork would remain the most visible. Informal carers, unregistered lodgers and people who distrusted institutions were represented mainly in private deposits and oral histories. Eda asked how much of that material the list preserved. Bas looked down at the slate. 'Very little,' he said. His embarrassment was more persuasive than a defence would have been.

The boy with the recorder was named Tavi. He asked whether his grandmother's recipes were in the archive. His father said this was not the time. Bas replied that it was exactly the time, although he could not promise that the recipes had been deposited. Tavi explained that his grandmother never measured the spice because she recognised its smell. If they saved the recipe without her explanation, he thought, it would not be a very good recipe. The nurse nodded. The adults had been discussing information; the child had described dependence between its parts.

Eda proposed preserving one small mandatory set: current medical information volunteered by the passengers, the catalogue itself and the archive's authentication keys. The remainder would be selected by a public draw among complete context bundles, weighted so that each bundle had the same chance per unit of storage. Large bundles would not be split merely because their survival was inconvenient. The method would not recognise importance. That was both its weakness and its purpose. Nobody could turn a position of authority aboard Parallax into the privilege of deciding whose past counted.

Bas objected that the draw might destroy irreplaceable evidence. Eda said every method would destroy irreplaceable evidence. A woman asked whether randomness was simply a way of avoiding responsibility. Eda considered that before replying. 'Only if we pretend the method chose itself. We would be choosing it, and recording why. I don't think we should call the result fair to the people whose records disappear.' The woman remained dissatisfied, but she stopped arguing that Eda was hiding behind a machine. It was the beginning of agreement, rather than its completion.

They adopted the proposal with conditions. Anyone could identify dependencies missing from the catalogue before the draw. The selection procedure and its starting value would be transmitted to the carrier before any plates were moved. A passenger, not Bas, would operate the selection program, and two others would check the physical loading order. Eda disclosed her mother's testimony and its location. The former manager disclosed records that might expose his own decisions. He had not wanted the inquiry preserved, he admitted. That admission changed the room more than any speech about solidarity could have done.

Fen interrupted to report a new constraint. Several cabinets had protective backing that could not enter the drive. Stripping it would take time they did not have if the plates were processed one at a time. They needed volunteers at three workstations. Nobody was to handle cracked ceramic without gloves. The meeting dissolved into practical groups, and the ethical dispute became a queue for tools. Eda watched Tavi's father join the team assigned to private deposits. He had no idea whether his mother's recipes were there. He began removing the frames anyway.

Before the draw, Bas took Eda aside. He had found her mother's bundle. It occupied less than a twentieth of the intact allowance. He could include it in the authentication material without anyone noticing; its records had been used to challenge the contractor's own data, so the classification would not be wholly indefensible. He did not offer the exception casually. He believed the inquiry might prevent the same abuses elsewhere. That made the offer harder to refuse. Simple corruption would have been easier to recognise than an exception supported by a cause she believed in.

Eda asked whether Bas would make the same offer to the woman seeking her father's voice. He said the consequences were different. She agreed. Then she said those consequences were precisely what they had decided not to let two people rank in private. Bas closed the catalogue. For several seconds she hated him for having put the possibility within reach. Afterwards she understood that she had been grateful to have somebody else to blame for the temptation. Her mother had not become less valuable when she refused. Refusal had merely become something she would have to live with.

The carrier confirmed receipt of the selection procedure. The nurse entered the starting value while the passenger compartment watched. Cabinet identifiers rolled down the screen. Some bundles were assigned to the intact reserve, others to the scan sequence, and the remainder to direct conversion. Eda found the ventilation inquiry halfway down the final group. Its companion maintenance logs had been selected for scanning. The distinction was devastatingly impersonal. Her mother's spoken account would be destroyed; some of the measurements that supported it might survive. She asked Irin to take her console for five minutes.

In the small washroom, Eda pressed her palms against the wall and tried to recall the exact cadence of her mother's voice. She could remember what it had said more easily than how it had sounded. This seemed a betrayal until she recognised it as one of the ordinary limits the archive had helped her postpone. There was no time to read the plates separately. The oscillator was already being transferred, and recalibrating it for a private preview would reduce the recoverable amount. She rinsed her face, dried the water from her wrists and returned to the bridge.

Irin did not ask whether she was ready. She asked Eda to verify the optical sight's alignment. The question gave her something she could answer. They checked the carrier beacon against two background sources and locked the reference. Fen reported that the conversion chamber was ready. Bas reported the loading order, with two passenger witnesses confirming each cabinet number. Eda read back the first pulse duration. Her mouth was dry, and she could hear the slight roughness in Irin's breathing. Competence did not abolish fear; it supplied fear with a sequence of tasks.

The first plates entered unread. Their destruction was needed to bring the chamber to its stable operating temperature before scanning could begin. On the cargo camera, they vanished between rollers without ceremony. Eda had expected some visual event proportionate to what was happening. Instead there was a pressure rise, a correction to the ship's orientation and a line of green indicators. She kept the beacon inside the sight's central bracket. Fen called the actuator delay. Irin counted the seconds until the next planned interruption. Below them, Bas said the first scanned bundle had been recovered.

It was a set of tenancy disputes concerning a corridor now open to vacuum. The carrier acknowledged the files and their authentication values. A passenger in the workshop cheered, then apologised, uncertain whether celebration was appropriate while other records were being destroyed. Bas told her not to apologise. The next bundle contained recordings of a school concert, a complaint about the concert's noise and the school's reply. Eda heard this inventory over the working channel and understood why context mattered. A vanished place had contained people who could dislike one another without either of them being wrong.

At the first long pulse, the port actuator lagged beyond the measured range. Fen called it immediately. Eda held the correction instead of adding another, waiting for the valve to move. The beacon slid towards the edge of the bracket. Her training urged an intervention that the previous simulation had shown would be excessive. She counted once, twice. The actuator responded. The beacon returned, though less neatly than she wanted. Irin marked the consumed margin. They had recovered it physically, but not mathematically: the next correction would have less room for error.

The scanner began reporting heat saturation. Its cooling loop shared a radiator with the drive controls, and the sustained pulse had warmed the return flow. Fen could reduce the scanning rate, bypass a sequence of plates or pause thrust while the loop cooled. Pausing would require a later pulse longer than the damaged actuator could safely sustain. They bypassed the next sequence. Bas read its identifiers aloud as it entered direct conversion. Eda asked why he was doing that. 'Because otherwise the log will only say temperature corrected,' he answered.

A sharp crack came over the cargo microphone. The rollers stopped. One plate had fractured diagonally and lodged across the feed throat, blocking both the scan path and the bypass. The chamber's reserve was falling. Fen shut the admission gate before the reaction became unstable. Eda watched their projected arrival move towards the edge of the carrier's receiving envelope. They had minutes to clear the obstruction, not hours. The archive was no longer merely something they were choosing to sacrifice. Its material resistance was now an immediate threat to everyone aboard.

The service hatch could be opened only after the throat had depressurised. Fen started the sequence, then discovered that the fractured plate was preventing the inner seal from seating. Bas proposed reaching through the access sleeve with a clamp. Fen rejected the clamp: if its jaws broke, its alloy would contaminate the chamber. Eda looked at the workshop feed. The protective frames they had removed lay stacked along one wall. Their ceramic spacers were compatible with the drive. Could they use a spacer as a wedge? Fen checked its composition label and said yes.

The nurse and Tavi's father held the access sleeve steady while Fen worked the wedge through it. Bas used the catalogue image to identify the plate's internal seam, a detail he had once dismissed as a manufacturing nuisance. Fen pressed there. The plate separated into two smaller pieces, both of which dropped into the bypass channel. She withdrew the sleeve before the seal closed. No one had performed an impossible feat. Four people had used information and materials that happened to remain available. Eda found that more moving than heroism would have been.

Restarting cost them another block of unread plates. Their revised trajectory still intersected the receiving envelope, but close to its outer limit. The carrier suggested releasing the intact reserve as inert mass to reduce the remaining braking requirement. Eda ran the calculation. It would help, though far less than feeding that material through the drive. The released cabinets would continue on their old trajectory into the belt. There would be no later rescue. Irin asked whether preserving the reserve still left a defensible arrival margin. Eda answered that it did, provided the last two pulses behaved within the new measured limits.

'And if they don't?' Irin asked. 'Then we use the bypass and increase feed. We destroy whatever remains in the scan queue.' The intact reserve was already secured away from the throat and could not be moved quickly enough to serve as an emergency correction. Irin considered the calculation, asked Fen for an independent assessment and kept the reserve aboard. It was a risk, but every available course now contained one. The relevant question was whether they understood its bounds, not whether they could describe their preferred option as safe.

While Fen reset the chamber, Bas discovered an error in the loading queue. Two crates had been exchanged after their frames were removed. One contained the ventilation inquiry. The other contained private deposits selected for direct conversion. Both were scheduled to disappear, so the exchange had not altered the draw's outcome. But the inquiry now stood beside the throat at the exact point where scanning was due to resume. Leaving it there would preserve Eda's mother's testimony while destroying a later bundle that had actually been selected. Nobody on the bridge would have known if Bas had remained silent.

He reported the error over the open channel. Eda closed her eyes for one breath, then thanked him. There was enough time to restore the order if the passengers shifted two crates together. She could see them doing it on the camera: ordinary backs bending, gloved fingers finding purchase, a label turned towards the verification lens. The decision she had made earlier was being made again in its physical form. It did not become easier through repetition. She concentrated on the sight while her mother's cabinet moved into the unread queue.

The penultimate pulse began. Eda's world narrowed to the beacon, the timing calls and Fen's reports. The drive shook harder than it had before the rupture. From the workshop came a sequence of file acknowledgements, each interrupted by the hiss of plates entering conversion. A maintenance technician's inspection notes survived. A family's holiday recordings did not. One bundle contained conflicting versions of a neighbourhood meeting, preserved together because nobody had agreed which minutes were accurate. Bas sounded almost amused when he announced it. Even under these conditions, the archive had refused to become a coherent monument.

Then the carrier's beacon flickered out. Eda froze the current setting. Irin called the backup frequency, and the carrier replied that its transmitter had switched power buses. The interruption would last several seconds. Automatic guidance would have extrapolated the target's position through the gap. Eda had tables and a secondary reference star, but the last actuator response had introduced uncertainty into their orientation. She could continue the pulse blind or cut it short. Continuing might save more records by avoiding an extra restart. She cut it short. The archive would absorb the cost of that choice.

The beacon returned after nine seconds. Fen reported sufficient chamber reserve for one restart, but the thermal margin for further scanning had gone. Eda verified the revised timing. Bas was already standing beside the bypass lever. He asked whether the interruption meant the rest of the selected scan queue would be lost. Irin said yes. Bas laid one hand on the final crate as if to steady himself. Then he pulled the lever. The scanner fell silent. Plates moved directly into the throat, and the ship began its last sustained deceleration.

Eda kept her eyes on the beacon. It drifted, settled and drifted again. Irin's calls were now spaced between Fen's warnings about the port actuator. Eda made the smallest corrections the valve would reliably accept. The ship's projected arrival entered the receiving envelope and continued towards its centre, but stopping at the centre was no longer possible without another correction they could not afford. She ended the pulse inside the boundary with the valve still functioning. On the display, insufficient braking reserve disappeared. In its place came rendezvous solution valid.

Nobody cheered on the bridge. Eda waited for the carrier to confirm the measured result rather than trust the prediction. The reply took four seconds. She would remember those seconds more clearly than the entire final burn: a loose screw trembling beside the pressure gauge, Irin's thumb pressed against a split in the console covering, a faint smell of hot dust. Then the carrier confirmed that a receiving boat was on its way. Eda unclipped her harness and discovered that her legs were too weak to support the confidence she had been performing.

Bas came up carrying the catalogue slate. They had preserved three tonnes intact and successfully decoded a little under two more. Some recovered files were damaged; those had been marked as incomplete rather than repaired into plausibility. More than half the archive was gone. Eda asked about the inquiry's maintenance logs. Two associated bundles had survived, including a sequence of alarm adjustments signed by the contractor's supervisor. The evidence might matter. It did not contain her mother's voice. Bas said he was sorry without trying to convert one fact into compensation for the other.

The receiving boat attached through the forward lock. Its crew brought fresh air cylinders and a list of instructions that seemed extravagantly ordinary. Passengers were to keep bags small, wear their transfer straps and leave the passage clear. Tavi asked whether the dog needed a strap. His father said yes, probably, and began searching for one. Eda watched the boy offer the dog his recorder as a distraction. The animal declined. For the first time since the tank rupture, something happened aboard Parallax that had no bearing on whether they would live.

Bas refused to leave until the intact cabinets had been secured for transfer. The relief crew initially classified them as nonessential cargo. Irin supplied their mass and attachment requirements, then informed the crew that the passengers had already paid more than enough for the distinction between essential and expendable. The boat could take the cabinets on a second trip. There was no need to abandon them now. Eda remained aboard with Bas while the others crossed. Through the lock's small window, she saw strangers become a receiving crowd, faces turning towards each new arrival.

Waiting for the second boat, Bas asked whether she regretted the draw. Eda said she regretted several of its results. He waited for her to distinguish that from regretting the decision itself. She could not give him the distinction cleanly. A method could remain defensible while its consequences hurt more than one had anticipated. Bas sat beside her on an empty restraint frame. Neither suggested that having survived entitled them to stop examining what they had done. When the docking signal sounded again, they rose together to guide the cabinets through the lock.

On the carrier, the archive was given a temporary berth in a room that had previously stored exercise equipment. Bas put a handwritten notice on the door: Incomplete collection. Catalogue includes destroyed holdings. Someone suggested removing the lost items from the public index to avoid disappointing researchers. He refused. A missing record was not the same as a record that had never existed. Eda helped him add the conversion log, the selection procedure and the names of those who had checked the loading. Their decisions became part of what later readers would have to examine.

The ventilation contractor's representatives challenged the surviving maintenance logs. They questioned the emergency reader, the chain of custody and Eda's involvement. These were questions she had expected, though expectation did not make them pleasant. The transmitted authentication values and the independently received conversion log established which files had survived without alteration. They did not establish every claim her mother had made. At the preliminary hearing, Eda resisted an invitation to describe the archive as complete evidence. She said precisely what it could support, and precisely what had been destroyed.

The hearing produced an order preserving the contractor's own remaining records. It was a beginning, not a verdict. Eda left the room feeling neither vindicated nor defeated. Outside, the former station manager waited to give his account of the decisions he had once hoped would disappear. He asked whether she wanted to hear it first. She said no; he should give it to the investigators in his own words. She had learned how tempting it was to shape testimony before it entered the record, especially when one believed the intended shape was true.

Several weeks later, Bas sent her a file recovered from the private deposits. It was a recording of a communal kitchen argument about whether a window should remain open. Eda's mother appeared briefly in the background, complaining that somebody had used the good scissors to cut wire. Her voice was distracted, mildly exasperated, entirely alive. The file did not restore her final statement. It did not make the draw providential. Had it belonged to another woman, its survival would have been no less valuable. Eda listened once, then sent a copy to her brother without adding an explanation.

When Parallax was cleared for repairs, Eda returned to retrieve the pressure gauge Irin had left on the bridge. The cargo hold was nearly empty. A fine ceramic dust remained along the edges of the feed throat, though the chamber itself had been cleaned. She resisted the impulse to collect some in a bag. It was not her mother, nor was it the station reduced to a symbol she could own. It was residue from a decision whose consequences would continue beyond her ability to measure them. She closed the service panel and signed the inspection record.

The archive opened to visitors on a quiet morning. Tavi came with his father to search for the recipes. They found none, but an elderly passenger offered to show him how she judged the spice by its smell. Bas asked permission to record their session. Tavi considered the request with unexpected seriousness, then agreed on condition that mistakes were kept in. Eda, waiting by the door, heard the recorder begin. There was a clatter of utensils, a question asked twice and laughter that obscured the first answer. The collection, irreparably diminished, acquired something new.

phrases.tr: kanıtın korunma ve el değiştirme kaydı

quiz.q: Why can the crew not simply copy the entire archive before destroying the plates?
options: Their portable storage is too small.
The records have no surviving catalogue.
Reading speed, cooling and the shared guidance oscillator impose limits.
The carrier refuses to receive civilian files.
quiz.explainTr: Sorun depolama kapasitesi değildir; okuma hızı, soğutma sınırı ve tek osilatörün rehberlik sistemiyle paylaşılması bütün arşivin kopyalanmasını engeller.

quiz.q: What is a principal objection to Bas's initial priority list?
options: It favours people already well represented in official paperwork.
It gives every context bundle an equal chance.
It excludes all engineering records.
It reserves most space for children's recipes.
quiz.explainTr: Resmî kayıtları öne alan liste, zaten kurumlarda daha görünür olan kişileri yeniden ayrıcalıklı kılar; özel anlatılarla temsil edilenler geri planda kalır.

quiz.q: Why does Eda reject the private exception for her mother's testimony?
options: She considers the testimony unreliable.
She believes the inquiry has already ended.
She knows another copy is aboard the carrier.
It would privately override the selection method agreed by the passengers.
quiz.explainTr: Eda tanıklığın önemini kabul eder ama iki kişinin özel kararıyla ortak yöntemin değiştirilmesini reddeder.

quiz.q: Why does Eda stop the pulse when the carrier's beacon disappears?
options: The archive reader has completed every selected file.
She prioritises a controlled arrival over saving the remaining scan queue.
She wants the carrier to move closer.
The optical sight no longer needs a reference.
quiz.explainTr: Eda belirsiz yönelimle itkiyi sürdürmek yerine güvenli yaklaşımı önceler; yeniden başlatmanın bedeli kalan tarama sırasının kaybıdır.

quiz.q: What does Bas's refusal to remove destroyed holdings from the catalogue express?
options: He expects every lost file to be reconstructed.
He wants to conceal the emergency selection.
Documented absence differs from pretending a record never existed.
He considers the surviving archive complete.
quiz.explainTr: Kayıp kayıtların katalogda kalması, neyin var olup yok edildiğini görünür tutar; kaybı hiç var olmamışlıkla eşitlemez.
